newsitem.title: USA: Toyota's Lexus to launch new age sport utility vehicle.
newsitem.headline: Toyota's Lexus to launch new age sport utility vehicle.

text.p: Stepping up its assault on the U.S. car market, Toyota Motor Corp. said Thursday it will launch a new car-based Lexus sport utility vehicle in 1998 aimed at buyers who want a truck's rugged image but not its rough ride.
Lexus unveiled a concept version of the new age sport utility vehicle at the Chicago Auto Show, which Lexus general manager James Press said closely resembles the production model.
The "Sport Luxury Vehicle" (SLV) concept is based on Lexus' ES300 luxury car chassis, not a heavy, full-frame truck chassis.
"This is the next movement," Press said. "People want the utility and sportiness of an SUV (sport utility vehicle) without the disadvantages."

Lexus' research showed that many people have shied away from sport utility vehicles because they often ride rough, have poor fuel economy and less-than-thrilling acceleration, and have high step-in height.

The SLV aims to solve that by offering a stylish body with luxury car ride, handling and comfort in a lightweight, fuel-efficient package. The vehicle is not designed for rugged off-road use, but most sport utility owners never take their vehicles off the pavement.
The vehicle is the latest in a growing trend among Japanese automakers to derive sport utility vehicles cheaply and quickly from existing car underpinnings.

Toyota's RAV4 small sport utility uses parts from the Toyota Celica car and Subuaru this year will introduce a sport utility based on its Legacy Outback wagon. Honda Motor Co. Ltd. is developing a sport utility based on its Accord sedan.
Auto analyst Michael Robinet of CSM Forecasting said he believed the production version of the SLV will be a big hit for Lexus.
"It hits their target market better than the LX450 did," he said referring to Lexus' big, rugged $48,000 sport utility vehicle derived from the Toyota Land Cruiser.
The LX450 will remain in the lineup for sport utility purists, Press said.

With sleek, muscular lines that resemble Chrysler Corp.'s Jeep Grand Cherokee and Mercedes-Benz' soon-to-be introduced, U.S-built M-Class vehicle, the SLV concept is designed to compete with them on price. Press said it will likely be priced in the "near luxury" range of $30,000 to $35,000.
Annual sales volume is expected to be about 22,000 to 42,000 units, which would make it Lexus's second-best selling vehicle behind the ES300.
The vehicle will enter production in the first half of 1998 at Toyota's most efficient factory, in Kyushu, Japan, and at this point is intended solely for the North American market.

In other introductions at the Chicago Auto Show Thursday, Chrysler Corp. debuted a four-door, extended-cab version of its Dodge Ram full-size pickup truck, which will be offered this fall as a 1998 model.

Chrysler, which pioneered a fourth door on its minivans, is the last of Detroit's Big Three to offer extra access doors on its pickup trucks -- Ford Motor Co.'s F-150 extended cab pickup offers a third door standard.
"If the other guys put three doors on, we like to do four," said Chrysler President Robert Lutz.
Ford is expected to follow suit with a fourth door on its F-150 this fall. "I think we're going to have a lot of fun with doors in the future," said Ford Division general manager Ross Roberts.
Ford also introduced a concept monster truck version of its F-Series pickup truck, aimed to be a precursor of a new heavier version of the truck aimed at commercial users.
The PowerForce, with meaty front-end styling reminiscent of Dodge's Ram pickup, uses a new V-10 engine that appeared in Ford full-size vans last fall.
